papers.title: Scalable Placement for Disaggregated LLM Serving on Heterogeneous Edge Fleets
papers.affiliations: University of Oslo, UiT The Arctic University of Norway

significance.reasoning: SPADE directly addresses LLM serving placement with exact optimization and strong empirical gains over heuristic baselines; its type-count dominance pruning and closed-form water-filling partitioner are concrete techniques worth evaluating for our own LLM serving scheduling/placement formulations.

papers.brief: SPADE tackles placement of disaggregated prefill/decode LLM serving on heterogeneous edge fleets, using a congestion-aware fluid tandem queue objective, type-count candidate enumeration with dominance pruning, and closed-form water-filling layer partitioning solved via multidimensional knapsack DP/MILP. On 30-device synthetic fleets it finds verified optimum in 441 ms while GA+DP takes 6855s with 19.7% higher congestion, and pruning eliminates 99.6% of candidates without observed loss. The key insight is that device-type symmetry plus dominance can make exact replica selection tractable, and the water-filling closed form replaces expensive layer DP—worth adopting in LLM serving placement optimization. It matters because it turns previously heuristic search into exact, fast optimization for heterogeneous serving.

methodology.core_method: Type-count candidate enumeration with dominance pruning, closed-form water-filling layer partitioning, and bounded multidimensional knapsack DP (or MILP fallback) over Pareto frontier of (PS, DS) throughputs minimizing fluid tandem-queue congestion W=CP+CD
methodology.novelty_claim: Dominance-based pruning plus type-count knapsack formulation and closed-form water-filling partitioning make exact congestion-aware placement tractable at fleet scale.

papers.title: SimpleEvol: An Agent-Loop Framework for LLM-Driven Automated Heuristic Design with Minimal Human Priors
papers.affiliations: Singapore Management University, National University of Singapore, Nanjing University of Information Science and Technology

significance.reasoning: The paper's AHI/ICE evaluation and minimal agent-loop baseline are directly relevant to LLM evolutionary search, with robust evidence over 10 models and 3 COPs. It does not force a change in our approach, but the metrics and SimpleEvol baseline are a concrete, useful benchmark to test whether added scaffolding actually converts model intelligence.

papers.brief: The paper proposes AHI (handcraftedness) and ICE (intelligence conversion efficiency) metrics and introduces SimpleEvol, a minimal single-trajectory agent loop for automated heuristic design that uses periodic history compression, meta-information feedback, and an elite best-so-far heuristic. Across 10 LLMs on TSP, CVRP, and FSSP, SimpleEvol achieves the highest ICE (e.g., 2.19 vs 1.82/1.51/0.82 on TSP and 6.21 vs 5.44/3.66/2.08 on CVRP against FunSearch/EoH/ReEvo) and generally lowest gaps, with leave-one-out and Bayesian-bootstrap robustness checks. The key insight is that less human-designed scaffolding may convert stronger LLM intelligence into heuristic quality more efficiently, suggesting evaluation should focus on scaling with model capability rather than final performance on fixed backbones. The ablation showing best-so-far retention and summarization are essential is worth extracting for lightweight LLM evolutionary search designs. This matters for LLM evolutionary search as it provides a competitive minimal baseline and a metric-based lens for framework complexity.

methodology.core_method: Minimal single-trajectory LLM agent loop: iterative code generation of heuristics conditioned on task description, elite heuristic, meta-information feedback (fitness, runtime, errors), and periodically compressed history summaries

methodology.novelty_claim: Introduces AHI (framework handcraftedness) and ICE (intelligence conversion efficiency) metrics and shows empirically that lower-handcraftedness AHD frameworks convert LLM intelligence into heuristic quality more efficiently, realized via a minimal agent-loop framework SimpleEvol.

papers.title: Optimal Scheduling of Multi-Site AI Data Centers in Day-Ahead Markets
papers.affiliations: National Laboratory of the Rockies

significance.reasoning: Solid LP formulation with GPU power caps for energy-aware data-center scheduling, well-evaluated on real CAISO data, but it is incremental over geographic load balancing and outside the primary LLM evolutionary search focus. Worth a skim for power-aware GPU scheduling, not a must-read.

papers.brief: Zhou and Cavraro present an LP that schedules GPU power caps, deferrable jobs, and online inference across three data-center sites to minimize day-ahead electricity cost, using 2025 CAISO prices and 210k GPUs. The 6.3% cost saving is decomposed into 3.8% price-independent efficiency, 2.3% temporal price response, and 0.2% spatial routing, backed by year-long simulation. The key transferable idea is the nested operating-mode decomposition, which prevents over-crediting power-cap efficiency as price-responsive flexibility—useful for any energy-aware scheduling evaluation. The piecewise-linear GPU throughput–power model is also a component worth incorporating into GPU scheduling formulations. It matters for energy-aware AI infrastructure scheduling, though it does not advance LLM evolutionary search.

methodology.novelty_claim: LP linking GPU power-cap levels and workload constraints to site facility power and locational DA prices, with nested operating modes that decompose savings into efficiency, temporal price response, and spatial routing.

papers.title: MetaShare: Failure-Aware Collective Self-Improvement for Open-Ended Agents
papers.affiliations: PwC

significance.reasoning: Directly advances LLM evolutionary search with a concrete, transferable memory design—signed mechanism-level records and failure-aware retrieval—backed by compute-matched ablations showing the memory/auditor account for speedups. Although baseline reuse and overlapping CIs temper effect-size claims, the component-level evidence and cross-domain breadth justify team attention.

papers.brief: MetaShare extends DGM-H-style open-ended self-improvement by persisting evaluated scaffold changes as signed mechanism-level records and retrieving successes and failures through separate channels; a task-blind auditor injects absent mechanism classes and parallel meta-agents propose at heterogeneous temperatures behind a deterministic gate. Across paper review, coding, math grading, robotics, and financial audit-risk, median final scores match or exceed DGM-H and reach the best agent 1.7–2.9× faster; compute-matched ablations show the memory and auditor—not extra proposals—drive the gains. The key takeaway is to store distilled, signed (helped/hurt) mechanism descriptions with performance deltas in a bounded cross-lineage pool, and use an avoid-channel plus coverage auditor to prevent redundant dead ends. The effect sizes should be read cautiously because some baseline numbers are inherited and CIs overlap, but the memory design is immediately implementable and relevant to LLM evolutionary search.

methodology.core_method: Archive-based evolutionary self-modification (DGM-H style) augmented with a bounded pool of signed mechanism-level meta-strategy records, asymmetric success/failure retrieval (DiverseTopK positives, BottomK worst failures), type-diverse retrieval, embedding de-ranking, task-blind LLM auditor injecting MUST-TRY categories, and K parallel meta-agents at heterogeneous temperatures behind a deterministic admissibility gate
methodology.llm_model_used: Claude Sonnet-4.5 (meta-agent, classifier), Claude Sonnet-4 (auditor), GPT o3-mini / GPT 4o-mini / GPT 4o (task agents)
methodology.novelty_claim: Makes the unit of cross-lineage sharing a signed, mechanism-level record with an explicit avoid-channel for failures, plus a task-blind auditor that steers mechanism-class coverage.

papers.title: eFAIR: Fair LLM Serving under Hourly Electricity Commitments
papers.affiliations: HKUST

significance.reasoning: eFAIR is a well-engineered LLM serving scheduler with strong empirical gains, but it proposes an online heuristic rather than a new OR formulation or methodological breakthrough. It is worth a team discussion for its normalized-throughput fairness metric and shared electricity-budget reservation scheme, especially for energy-constrained LLM serving scheduling.

papers.brief: eFAIR is an online LLM serving scheduler that coordinates request dispatching, electricity budget allocation, and GPU frequency selection to maximize leximin-fair normalized request throughput under an hourly electricity commitment. Results on H20 and H200 configurations with 32 replicas show 28.0%-31.0% higher tenth-percentile normalized throughput than the best budget-feasible baseline, with absolute commitment deviation below 0.26%. The key insight is using a common normalized-throughput target to align request priority, future electricity reservations, and frequency choices, with surplus electricity used to accelerate higher-entitlement requests. This matters for energy-constrained LLM serving and GPU resource-allocation research, though it has little relevance to LLM evolutionary search.

methodology.novelty_claim: Formulates fair LLM serving as leximin optimization of entitlement-normalized throughput under an hourly electricity commitment, jointly coordinating dispatching, budget reservation, and GPU frequency selection.

papers.title: Coordinating Distributed AI Servers with Industrial Loads to Reduce Grid-Interconnection Needs
papers.affiliations: Columbia University

significance.reasoning: The paper applies a standard MILP to AI server sizing/scheduling/routing, which overlaps with our OR-for-AI infrastructure work but introduces no new methods or challenges to our approaches. Its empirical contribution is specific to grid-interconnection capacity rather than LLM serving or GPU scheduling.

papers.brief: Lyu and Xu formulate a joint MILP for sizing CPU/GPU server groups, scheduling deadline-constrained firm/flexible AI tasks, and routing tasks across factories to minimize annualized server, interconnection, and energy costs. Using 2030 demand projections and measured hourly production loads for 31 Chinese manufacturing industries, they report that factory-site deployment reduces additional grid-interconnection capacity by 60–63% versus new data centers, and by 98% with cross-site routing, from 1,488 MW to 30 MW nationally. Results are backed by public code and real load data, though the analysis is deterministic and routing benefits are an unconstrained upper bound. The key transferable insight is that co-locating AI workloads with existing heterogeneous loads and exploiting non-coincident peak capacity can substantially reduce infrastructure requirements. This is relevant to OR for AI infrastructure, but its contribution is an application-specific MILP case study rather than a methodological advance for LLM serving or GPU scheduling.

methodology.novelty_claim: Quantifies that co-locating AI servers at factory sites and coordinating AI workloads with production loads (including cross-site routing) cuts required additional grid interconnection by 60-98% versus new large data centers.

papers.brief: Albrecht et al. use Claude Code with only open-source tools to author scheduling solvers for job shop, flexible job shop, and FJSP with transport robots. Results are backed by independent checkers, all-run reporting, and repeated sessions: they reach 525,515 on the 100,000-operation tai_100_1000_1, improve all ten 100x1000 instances, 11 Behnke instances, and 7 MKT instances versus commercial baselines. The key transferable insight is that the agent autonomously identifies exploitable instance structure and changes formulation—e.g., a fixed-target corridor min-conflicts search—and can leave a reusable specialized solver that transfers to similar instances. This matters as evidence that frontier LLM coding agents, even without evolutionary search or task-specific frameworks, can beat general commercial solvers on structured scheduling benchmarks, though transfer to machine-dominated instances is weak.

papers.title: Reducing Batch Makespan for LLM Agent Workloads through Inference-Environment Coordination
papers.affiliations: Ant Group

significance.reasoning: Solid empirical systems work on batch makespan for LLM agent serving, directly relevant to our LLM serving scheduling thread, but methods are incremental engineering heuristics rather than formal OR or LLM-evolutionary-search advances.

papers.brief: Feng et al. propose coordinated inference-environment optimizations for batch execution of multi-turn LLM agent tasks, including a workload-aware hybrid-cache allocation model, trajectory-label-based routing/scheduling, and capacity separation with Chain-Advancing Action Scheduling. Live experiments with Ling-3.0/3.1-Flash on BFCL, SWE-bench Multilingual, WideSearch, and MCP-Atlas report 10.4–65.0% makespan reductions with aligned scores, and controlled replay isolates individual optimizations. The key insight is that separating sample admission from environment execution and scheduling pending environment jobs by observed chain progress can substantially improve GPU utilization and shorten batch tails under constrained tool capacity. The workload-aware cache model also provides a simple way to choose cache ratio and concurrency for hybrid LLMs. This is useful for LLM serving scheduling but is not central to LLM evolutionary search methods.

papers.title: AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
papers.affiliations: MIT CSAIL

significance.reasoning: AutoAssumption introduces assumption-level search with Lean-verified proof graphs and shows it matches OpenEvolve/AIDE at equal budget with lower variance, while producing SOTA results in two ML-systems fields. This directly challenges code-level LLM evolutionary search and provides a concrete alternative genotype worth evaluating in our own algorithm discovery work.

papers.brief: Sadalski et al. formalize 89 ML-systems algorithms as Lean-checked proof graphs with explicit assumptions, then use an LLM harness to relax one assumption at a time, re-derive only the affected proof statements, and generate new code. The results are backed by substantial benchmarking: their discovered variants achieve state-of-the-art RULER-4K scores for KV-cache eviction and lowest WikiText-2 perplexity for weight pruning, and at equal budget the harness scores within 0.4 points of OpenEvolve with much lower variance across repeats. The key insight is that treating assumptions as the searchable unit, rather than raw code edits, makes each design change attributable, reproducible, and checkable via proof, which improves search stability and interpretability. For LLM evolutionary search, this suggests incorporating assumption-level proof graphs as a structured search space could complement or improve code-level evolution, especially where correctness is critical. The work is relevant because it directly competes with AlphaEvolve-style code search and offers a practical blueprint for proof-guided algorithm discovery.

papers.title: COMPASS: Composable Policy-Amortized Structured Search for LLM-Based Optimization Modeling
papers.affiliations: Hanoi University of Science and Technology, VinMotion

significance.reasoning: Solid autoformulation result with real benchmark gains and McNemar significance, but it is adjacent to rather than directly competitive with evolutionary search or OR-for-AI work; the transferable piece is learned amortized graph traversal, not a method we would immediately adopt.

papers.brief: COMPASS treats optimization-template retrieval for LLM autoformulation as a sequential decision process over a template DAG, learning a DQN traversal policy from LLM structural judgments and solver-execution feedback. Across six optimization-modeling benchmarks and several LLM backbones, it improves over OptiTree, SolverLLM, and AutoFormulator, with the largest gains on complex compositional problems; paired McNemar tests against a DAG-greedy baseline are statistically significant. The key insight is that semantic node embeddings make the policy extendable to newly inserted templates without redefining the action space, while a lightweight LLM compatibility prior regularizes sparse feedback. This matters for generative AI for OR because it shifts retrieval from per-instance search to amortized learned navigation, though single-run results and missing compute/code details limit reproducibility.

papers.title: From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings
papers.affiliations: MIT, Tsinghua, UC San Diego, Tongji, Peking University, McGill, Northeastern

significance.reasoning: Solid benchmark work for OR clarification and LLM evaluation; the regret-label/twin-control design is a concrete idea worth discussing for ambiguity-grounded OR benchmarking, but it does not change our primary LLM evolutionary search approach.

papers.brief: Tang et al. introduce Ask2Decide, a 43-task benchmark where an LLM agent must elicit hidden operational facts from an operator before submitting an optimization plan. The key methodological contribution is using a solver to label each missing fact by minimax regret and pairing relevant facts with zero-value twins, while scoring initial plans separately from post-feedback recovery. On four frontier LLMs, initial plans are infeasible on 58–98% of tasks when information is missing versus 5–28% with full information, and agents uncover relevant facts only 5–12 points more often than twins. They also collect 79 human operator sessions and build CalOp, a simulated operator calibrated to mimic human withholding behavior. For OR benchmarking and interactive optimization evaluation, the regret-label/twin-control design is a useful standard, though it is not directly relevant to LLM evolutionary search.

papers.title: Spot Markets for AI Inference: Dynamic Capacity Allocation and Pricing on a Shared Accelerator Fleet
papers.affiliations: New York University

significance.reasoning: Directly relevant to LLM inference capacity allocation and scheduling, with solid LP/MPC formulation and a useful batching-induced latency exchange rate, but it does not impact the primary LLM evolutionary search direction and relies on stylized simulations. A focused discussion could evaluate whether the latency exchange rate and shadow-price pricing rules should be incorporated into LLM serving scheduling cost models.

papers.brief: The paper formulates dynamic spot pricing and placement for a shared LLM inference fleet as a model-predictive-control problem solved by a small LP, deriving a batching-induced latency exchange rate, optimal slack pricing, backfill reliability, and placement hysteresis. Numerical results are backed by paired simulations with 20 random draws and standard errors, showing a 7.4% profit gain over fixed half-price practice and capturing 93% of the perfect-forecast gain on a stylized 512-accelerator week. The key insight is that continuous batching turns interactive-vs-spot capacity into a linear displacement constraint, with one interactive token per second displacing rho_m > 1 spot tokens per second, making pricing and placement tractable through shadow prices. This is relevant to LLM serving scheduling and resource allocation because it provides a principled cost/price model for latency tiers, deadlines, and power caps, though it does not address LLM evolutionary search or multi-agent coordination.

methodology.core_method: Model predictive control solving a per-period linear program (piecewise-linear revenue segments, tangent cuts on expected normal overflow, cumulative deadline constraints) with receding horizon
methodology.novelty_claim: Derives a latency exchange rate between interactive and spot tiers from continuous batching and embeds closed-form pricing, backfill, and placement-hysteresis results into a millisecond LP-based MPC for inference capacity.

papers.title: SwarmEvolve: Latent Agent Swarms for Evolutionary Discovery and Optimization

significance.reasoning: Directly targets LLM evolutionary search scalability with a novel latent reasoning/KV-cache crossover and latent novelty filter. The 5-13x throughput gains and small-model AlphaEvolve matches are backed by 3-seed, multi-benchmark experiments and code release.

papers.brief: SwarmEvolve replaces text-based reasoning in LLM-guided evolution with 450 latent agents per round that reason in embedding space and pass KV caches; a latent farthest-point novelty filter selects diverse trajectories, and summarizer agents decode candidate programs. On 21 mathematical discovery and scientific computing problems, it achieves higher mean scores than OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, and CodeEvolve across Qwen3 8B/14B/32B-FP8, reaches their 60-minute best scores in 3-8 minutes, and with Qwen3 8B improves several AlphaEvolve constructions. Results are backed by three seeds per problem, ablations replacing latent steps with text, and exact-constraint re-evaluation. The key transferable insight is that latent reasoning and KV-cache concatenation provide built-in diversity and crossover at much lower cost than text, with novelty filtering done directly on hidden states. This is a significant scalability improvement for LLM evolutionary search.

methodology.core_method: Evolutionary program search where 10 swarms of 45 latent-reasoning LLM agents (450/round) reason in embedding space for 40 steps, communicate via concatenated KV caches (RoPE-rotated) to a summarizer that writes programs; greedy farthest-point novelty filter in latent space keeps 30/45 agents
methodology.novelty_claim: Large-scale swarms of low-cost agents that reason and communicate entirely in latent space (KV-cache passing) with a latent-space novelty filter, enabling built-in crossover and 5-13x higher throughput than text-based evolutionary frameworks.

papers.title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
papers.affiliations: HKUST, University of Southern California

significance.reasoning: Solid queueing-theoretic scheduling method with real H800 GPU validation, directly relevant to LLM serving scheduling work and offering an implementable cμ/backfill baseline. It is incremental over existing fluid-guided memory-constrained policies (WAIT/SVF), assumes known output lengths and single-GPU, so it is worth tracking and testing rather than a must-read or thinking-changing result.

papers.brief: Li et al. develop a fluid-limit queueing model for LLM inference scheduling under KV-cache memory constraints and prove that a cμ priority rule with effective service rates minimizes holding cost and completion time; they also introduce a smoothed cμ-inspired policy for finite systems. On an NVIDIA H800 with production traces, cμ-backfill reduces average latency from 35.5s to 9.5s on To-B and from 30.2s to 10.4s on semi-synthetic workloads compared with vLLM, while remaining competitive with or better than SVF/MC-SF/WAIT. The key transferable idea is to compute effective service rates from prefill compute, KV-cache I/O, and memory capacity, then use cμ ordering plus future-KV feasibility checks for admission and backfilling. This is a relevant, theory-backed scheduling method for LLM serving under memory constraints; it does not change LLM evolutionary search approaches.

significance.reasoning: Solid formalization of zero-marginal groups and learning-augmented staged search for Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition selection, with rigorous theory and strong experiments. papers.brief: The paper proves that finding hidden zero-marginal constraint-family groups in Dantzig-Wolfe decomposition requires Θ(k^w) bound evaluations, and shows that a staged search using an LLM-predicted group with e misses reduces cost to Θ(k^e), with an interleaved order preserving robustness. Results are backed by exact computations, a MIPLIB-NL census, and branch-and-price solve-time measurements, not just claims. The key takeaway is that a predictor's value can be measured as evaluation savings, and interleaving a prediction-guided order with a covering order bounds the loss from wrong predictions, a pattern transferable to expensive-evaluation optimization loops. This matters for LLM-in-the-loop MILP strengthening and column-generation workflows, but it is adjacent to, rather than a direct advance in, LLM evolutionary search.

papers.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
papers.affiliations: UC Berkeley, Princeton, Stanford, NVIDIA

significance.reasoning: SpecPilot provides a concrete, validated recipe for ceiling-guided multi-agent search with token-forcing evaluation integrity, directly addressing sample efficiency and reward hacking in LLM evolutionary search. The cost-model and structured-memory components are worth discussing for adoption in agentic optimization pipelines.

papers.brief: SpecPilot applies an autonomous, ceiling-guided agentic loop to optimize speculative decoding per deployment. It decomposes speedup into token acceptance, kernel, and overhead factors, then parallel sub-agents implement patches, a controller promotes statistically significant gains, and token forcing rejects lossy changes; validated mechanisms persist in structured memory across deployments. Results are backed by paired runs on 4 target models, 3 drafters, 2 GPUs, and 5 benchmarks, raising speedup over AR from stock 4.46x to 10.87x single-request and 1.94x to 3.93x batched, with clear ablation against a single-agent loop. The key transferable insight is ceiling-guided search: explicitly estimate the largest performance gap at each round to redirect evolutionary exploration, and use stock-calibrated token forcing as a robust reward-hacking filter. This matters for LLM evolutionary search and systems optimization because it demonstrates how to scale agentic discovery beyond toy problems with reliable evaluation and memory reuse.

papers.title: Layer-wise CPU-GPU Scheduling for LLM Inference on Memory-Limited Consumer GPUs
papers.affiliations: Keio University, SoftBank Corp.

significance.reasoning: This is solid work on LLM inference scheduling with strong empirical speedups, but it is a lightweight analytical heuristic rather than a fundamental OR formulation, and it is not directly relevant to LLM evolutionary search. The transfer-hiding idea is worth noting for offloading placement, but we would not change our current approach.

papers.brief: This paper presents a layer-wise CPU/GPU placement and scheduling method for LLM inference on memory-limited single-GPU systems. It models decode latency as max(total computation, total transfer) after relaxing transfer timing constraints and uses a continued-fraction search to choose the ratio of CPU-executed layers to GPU streamed layers. On a consumer RTX 5090, it reports 3.5x speedup over HuggingFace Accelerate and 6.3x over DeepSpeed ZeRO-Inference for OPT-30B, hiding 99.6% of transfers; however, it is 22% slower than SplitGen for Llama2-70B under host-memory pressure. The key insight is that CPU computation during batch-size-1 decode can be deliberately used as a planned window to hide weight transfers, with simple average-based ratio balancing providing strong offloading gains. This is relevant to LLM serving scheduling, but it is not a fundamental advance and lacks code release and statistical rigor.

methodology.core_method: Latency model L=max(C(m),W(m)) with relaxed transfer constraints; continued-fraction search to find integer ratio x:y of CPU vs stream layers balancing avg CPU compute time and avg transfer time; layer placement into cpu/resident/stream modes with async pinned-memory weight prefetch hidden behind CPU computation
methodology.novelty_claim: Uses CPU-executed layers as planned computation windows to hide weight transfers during batch-size-1 decode, with layer placement optimized via a relaxed latency model reduced to a ratio-balancing integer problem.

papers.title: Queuing for Inference: Dynamic Memory Footprints and Costly Preemption
papers.affiliations: Purdue University

significance.reasoning: Directly relevant to queueing/OR for LLM serving scheduling, with solid analytical and simulation results, but it is a theoretical single-server model unlikely to change current GPU scheduling approaches or code.

papers.brief: This paper introduces a queueing model for LLM inference serving that couples attained-service-dependent KV-cache growth, finite memory capacity with service slowdown, and memory-proportional preemption overhead. It shows that classical Gittins scheduling can become unstable under costly preemption and proposes MLPT, a multi-level age-threshold policy with derived mean response time and an empirical rule for threshold selection. Simulations over 100,000 jobs show 15–50% mean response time reductions over FCFS and stable behavior where capped Gittins degrades. The key insight is that optimal scheduling balances short-job priority against memory-dependent preemption overhead, with the memory slowdown threshold serving as a natural preemption point in limited-memory regimes. This is relevant for LLM serving scheduling theory but remains an analytical/simulation study without real-system validation.

However, the domain is far from algorithm discovery/OR, and the lack of code release limits direct adoption.

papers.title: Harnessing Language Models as Optimization Modeling Agents
papers.affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, Huawei

significance.reasoning: Solid empirical study in LLM optimization modeling with large benchmark coverage and several adapted baselines; relevant to our OR modeling evaluation work but not to LLM evolutionary search, and it lacks code release and uncertainty quantification.

papers.brief: Luo et al. propose two frozen-LLM inference harnesses for natural-language optimization modeling: OptiCycle runs a persistent Python loop of code generation, execution, and revision; OptiState adds an explicit five-element formulation as revisable state. Across nine benchmarks and 2,634 problems with 11 Qwen models, OptiCycle improves macro accuracy by up to 49.46 points and outperforms six adapted agentic workflows and several post-trained OR models under shared backbones. The results are quantitative and appear real, though they are point estimates without confidence intervals, method-specific budgets confound some comparisons, and no code is released. The key takeaway is that a simple execution-and-repair harness—rather than complex multi-agent or fine-tuned systems—can capture most of the gains on LLM optimization modeling, while explicit formulation state helps inconsistently. This is informative for LLM-based OR modeling and evaluation, but its findings are less transferable to LLM evolutionary search for algorithm design.

papers.title: Directing to Diversify: Multi-Directional Search for Automatic Heuristic Design
papers.affiliations: Singapore Management University, Nanyang Technological University, University of Zurich, ETH Zurich, Eindhoven University of Technology, A*STAR

significance.reasoning: PRS directly targets LLM-based automatic heuristic design with a novel generation-level directional operator set and shows consistent, statistically significant gains over MCTS-AHD and EoH; the idea-level expansion/compression/steering primitive is actionable for our LLM evolutionary search pipelines but not a fundamental paradigm shift.

papers.brief: Zhu et al. propose PRS, an LLM-based automatic heuristic design method that applies three directional idea-level perturbations—expansion, compression, and steering—before rewriting code, organized in bounded BFS with UCB operator selection and stagnation restart. On CVRP, KP, OBPP, TSP, and FSSP, PRS reduces optimality gaps relative to MCTS-AHD and EoH, e.g., CVRP-50 0.79% vs 1.54%, KP-100 0.02% vs 0.05%, with statistical significance and strong OOD generalization, while using fewer LLM queries than MCTS-AHD. The key insight is that deliberately diversifying heuristic structure at the idea level along complementary semantic directions sustains exploration better than generic EC-style mutation. This directly informs LLM evolutionary search over code: the expansion/compression/steering decomposition is a simple, transferable primitive worth testing in other program-synthesis pipelines.

significance.reasoning: Directly relevant controlled ablation of memory, agenda, and repulsion in LLM evolutionary search, with results showing memory+repulsion prevents collapses but gains are additive and unresolved at n=9. papers.brief: Ono Filho instruments a minimal FunSearch-style loop with a 2^3 factorial of proposer-side operator packages—schematic notebook memory, obstacle agenda, behavioral repulsion—across nine construction problems. Results are real but modest: the full composition improves gap-closed by +0.196 (nominal p=0.023, but stage-combination p≈0.08), repulsion raises construction-hash diversity in eight of nine problems, and memory+repulsion is the only arm that never collapses; however no per-term effect survives correction at n=9. Key insight: memory and repulsion compose additively, with memory providing collapse insurance rather than superadditive gain, and a frontier proposer reaches similar plateaus with ~20x fewer samples, suggesting proposer strength dominates operator tweaks at office scale. This matters for LLM evolutionary search as a reproducible, pre-registered ablation of operator-level interventions and a caution that gains may be local-proposer phenomena; the released code and data make the findings actionable.

papers.title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization

significance.reasoning: ORSMT provides exact SMT-based semantic verification and repair for LLM-generated optimization models, with strong large-scale results. It is directly relevant to LLM OR modeling evaluation but does not advance core LLM evolutionary search or multi-agent optimization methods.

papers.brief: ORSMT introduces SMT-based exact semantic verification and repair for LLM-generated optimization artifacts, comparing source requirements, mathematical formulations, solver code, and reports. Results are substantial and backed by large-scale experiments: on 3,034 problems it lifts model–code matches from 43.2% to 88.2% and correct-and-matched outputs from 25.2% to 40.2%, with median sub-second checks through 99 constraints. The key transferable insight is using SMT violation queries to certify or refute semantic equivalence via projected feasible regions and objective preferences, yielding localized counterexamples that drive effective repair. This is useful for LLM-based optimization modeling and benchmarking but less directly relevant to evolutionary search or multi-agent optimization.

papers.affiliations: AWS AI Labs, Georgia Institute of Technology

significance.reasoning: Directly targets LLM evolutionary search by making the campaign policy itself an evolvable artifact, with strong held-out results and ablation evidence. However, single search runs, no significance tests, and no public code temper the strength of the claim, so it merits team discussion on transferring the bounded-environment and meta-evolved skill approach to our algorithm-discovery frameworks rather than immediately changing our approach.

papers.brief: FREEEVOLVE replaces fixed search loops in LLM-driven agent harness evolution with an evolver that autonomously controls task selection, evaluation repetitions, branching, and stopping, guided by an editable markdown skill; an outer meta-evolver improves that skill by judging it on the workers its full campaigns produce. Across four benchmarks, the meta-evolved skill improves held-out metrics by 2.2 to 13.8 points over the seed and matches or exceeds hand-designed evolvers on six of seven metrics, with ablations and traces supporting adaptive resource allocation and token efficiency. The key transferable idea is treating the evolution campaign policy itself as an evolvable artifact and meta-evolving it via full inner runs, which could be applied to LLM evolutionary search frameworks beyond agent harnesses. Results are credible but based on single search runs with no significance testing and no public code yet, and transfer degrades on dissimilar hardware. For this research area, it is a strong direction-setting preprint rather than an immediate recipe.

methodology.core_method: Claude Code agent invoked once with an editable markdown 'evolution skill' that autonomously controls the whole improvement campaign (task selection, repetitions, concurrency, timeouts, branching, stopping); the skill itself is meta-evolved by an outer evolver that scores candidate skills by the workers their full campaigns produce

methodology.novelty_claim: Treats the hand-designed search loop of agent evolvers as a learnable campaign policy (an editable evolution skill) that is meta-evolved by evaluating candidate skills through complete worker-evolution campaigns.

papers.title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
papers.affiliations: MBZUAI, Carnegie Mellon University, Hong Kong Baptist University, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, University of Sydney

significance.reasoning: Directly targets sample efficiency and persistent experience reuse in LLM evolutionary search via LLM-discovered idea factors, with strong empirical results on 11 math and 6 MLE tasks. The approach is worth discussing, though 3 seeds, no significance tests, and no released code limit the weight of the conclusions.

papers.brief: ExpEvolve augments an SCS-style evolutionary coding agent with LLM-discovered high-level 'idea factors' that explain score differences between programs, then uses a soft-UCB bandit over ADD/REMOVE/SET actions to exploit them while maintaining random and plateau-triggered exploration. Across 11 mathematical discovery tasks and 6 MLS-Bench tasks, it reports better final scores than SCS and ShinkaEvolve, with 1.7-26.2x fewer evaluations on selected tasks, and transfers across four LLMs. The core transferable insight is to structure memory as semantically meaningful binary/categorical factors learned from unexplained pairwise score contrasts, rather than program-level summaries, and to allocate mutation budget via a bandit over those factors. Results are numerically reported but based on 3 seeds with no significance tests or code release, so they are promising rather than definitive. It matters for LLM evolutionary search because it directly addresses sample efficiency and experience reuse, two central bottlenecks in open-ended discovery.

methodology.core_method: Evolutionary coding agent (SCS backbone) augmented with LLM-discovered idea factors: pairwise ridge ranker over idea annotations, unexplained-pair-driven factor proposal, soft-UCB multi-armed bandit over ADD/REMOVE/SET idea actions, plateau-triggered background probing and masking
methodology.novelty_claim: Introduces idea-level (high-level factor) experience extraction and bandit-controlled reuse in evolutionary coding agents, with theory on when idea factors improve sample efficiency and when exploration degenerates.

papers.title: Beyond Experience: Knowledge-Guided Evolution for NPU Kernel Generation
papers.affiliations: Shenzhen Loop Area Institute, CUHK-Shenzhen, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Guangzhou University, Southwestern University of Finance and Economics

significance.reasoning: Solid application of LLM evolutionary search with a transferable external-knowledge grounding idea, but domain-specific and single-run evidence; not a fundamental change. The concrete action is to evaluate version-aware external knowledge bases for broadening mechanism diversity in LLM evolutionary search.

papers.brief: AscendEvolve grounds LLM evolutionary kernel generation in a version-aware external knowledge base (platform docs, headers, vendor libraries) using hierarchical demand-driven retrieval, then evolves mechanism-distinct implementation lines with tree exploration and mechanism-level crossover. On 53 Ascend C operators, it reports 71.39 overall score (+11.6% over Reflexion, +17.2% over OpenEvolve), with ablation showing the knowledge base nearly doubles L3 score; results are real but single-run with no variance and no code release. The key insight is that external knowledge can overcome 'experience closure' in LLM evolutionary search: version-checked retrieval seeds mechanisms beyond what self-generated memory contains and makes more planned strategies survive correctness filtering (5x increase in full-correct strategy survival). This idea is transferable to LLM evolutionary search for algorithm design, where injecting structured domain knowledge could similarly broaden mechanism diversity and reduce wasted samples. The paper matters as a strong application of knowledge-grounded evolution, but not as a fundamental advance in evolution operators or sample efficiency.

methodology.core_method: Knowledge-grounded two-stage evolutionary LLM agent: hierarchical demand-driven retrieval (route/filter/read) over versioned platform KB + per-operator KB, tree-based exploration of M mechanism-distinct lines with planner/coder/debugger/evaluator roles, then mechanism-level crossover with KB compatibility check
methodology.novelty_claim: Grounds every stage of evolutionary kernel search in a large version-aware external platform knowledge base with demand-driven retrieval and bidirectional knowledge-experience feedback, instead of relying only on self-generated experience memory.

papers.title: SpecEvo: Speculative Evolution with Large Language Models for Cost-Efficient Scientific Discovery
papers.affiliations: National University of Singapore, Hanoi University of Science and Technology

significance.reasoning: SPECEVO is a strong, directly relevant cost-efficient multi-LLM evolutionary framework with broad empirical validation, but it combines existing components (MAP-Elites, multi-model routing, guidance) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism, so it does not change our thinking. The Advisor failure-memory and stagnation-triggered Navigator design is concrete enough to discuss adopting for sample efficiency.

papers.brief: SPECEVO coordinates lightweight parallel Speculators, a lightweight Advisor, and sparse frontier-model Navigator interventions by consolidating trajectory evidence from successes, failures, and saturated niches. Across 176 tasks spanning mathematics, systems optimization, combinatorial optimization, and scientific equation discovery, it matches or outperforms frontier-only and cost-efficient baselines while reducing API cost by 50–80% and improving the strongest CO-Bench baseline by 3.8%. Results are backed by three runs, bootstrap confidence intervals, and matched-budget comparisons. The key transferable idea is using rolling, failure-grounded guidance and a stagnation signal to select among synthesis, surgical repair, and reframing at sparse checkpoints, with stochastic guidance injection to avoid herding. This is directly relevant to improving sample and cost efficiency in LLM evolutionary search.

methodology.core_method: Asynchronous multi-LLM evolutionary search (speculate-then-consolidate): parallel lightweight Speculators with MAP-Elites archive (AST+description PCA descriptors, periodic refit), stagnation-adaptive Zipf parent sampling, six variation prompts, lightweight Advisor producing rolling guidance, and sparse frontier Navigator selecting synthesis/surgical/reframe

significance.reasoning: Solid benchmark and inference-time method for soft-constraint LLM autoformulation, relevant to our OR modeling evaluation work, but it is an incremental adaptation of AST-guided translation and does not alter our core approach.

papers.brief: Goel et al. introduce ASTOR, an inference-time framework that prompts an LLM to emit a grammar-guided AST, which is deterministically validated and compiled to Gurobi, along with SoftOR, a benchmark for weighted-penalty and lexicographic soft-constraint autoformulation. On 355 SoftOR instances ASTOR reaches 88.5% solution accuracy versus 84.8% for the strongest baseline and remains competitive on hard-constraint benchmarks; results include bootstrap confidence intervals and cost/error analyses, making the empirical claims credible. The key transferable idea is that constraining LLM outputs to a formal, adequacy-proven optimization grammar and compiling them deterministically reduces formulation errors, especially for ordered preferences. This is relevant for LLM autoformulation research and evaluation, though it is an incremental extension of AST-based translation rather than a fundamental new search or optimization method.

papers.title: Hyper Algorithm Design Agent: Evolving Learnable Optimizer from Zero
papers.affiliations: South China University of Technology, South China Normal University, Singapore Management University

significance.reasoning: HADA directly targets automated MetaBBO algorithm design with a dual-agent self-modifying code-evolution framework, which is squarely in LLM evolutionary search but largely combines known ideas from Hyperagents/Darwin Gödel Machine with LLaMEA-style optimization code editing. The empirical gains are plausible but rely on relative-improvement framing and lack significance tests, so it is worth a team discussion on adopting self-referential prompt evolution, not a must-read.

papers.brief: HADA introduces a dual-agent LLM coding framework where a hyper agent edits a task agent (and itself) to evolve a MetaBBO codebase from a naive DQN-DE template, guided by a tree-based archive and normalized per-problem scores. On COCO-BBOB, the evolved algorithm achieves a 0.967 average score versus 0.894 for the best MetaBBO baseline (GLEET) after 100 evolution steps, but the claimed 121.7% 'leap' is a relative framing and constrained/multi-objective results are only shown as bar charts. The key transferable idea is the explicit separation of a self-modifying hyper agent from a code-editing task agent, coupled with an algorithm evolution tree, which makes open-ended design of learnable optimizers practically implementable. This matters for LLM evolutionary search because it demonstrates a working recursive self-improvement loop over optimization codebases, even though the core mechanisms are borrowed from prior open-endedness systems.

papers.title: PRECOCIAL: Pretraining with Code Curriculums via Iterative Search for Accelerated Learning
papers.affiliations: Cornell University, Cisco Research

significance.reasoning: Directly targets LLM-guided program search with expensive training-based fitness, and the continual-pretraining-with-rollback mechanism is a concrete, well-ablated efficiency improvement over FunSearch/AlphaEvolve. Not field-changing, but relevant to sample efficiency in AlphaEvolve-style search and worth a team discussion on applying the technique to expensive candidate evaluations.

papers.brief: Gu et al. introduce PRECOCIAL, an LLM-guided iterative search that optimizes Python programs generating synthetic pretraining data, scored by fine-tuning a small transformer on the generated data and measuring downstream validation perplexity. The key efficiency idea is to continue pretraining a single network across accepted candidate programs and roll back checkpoints on rejection, rather than training a fresh network for every candidate as FunSearch and AlphaEvolve do. On four language/code datasets and four reasoning tasks, optimized programs beat hand-designed curricula, procedural generators, random mutation, and first-iteration LLM programs, and also outperform FunSearch and AlphaEvolve at matched evaluation budget with about 2.5x fewer pretraining steps; results are supported by paired statistical tests and ablations showing the continued network is the source of the gain. For LLM evolutionary search with training-based fitness, the transferable insight is to reuse a single continuously updated model across candidates with rollback, improving both sample efficiency and final quality. This matters for anyone applying AlphaEvolve-style search to problems where evaluating a candidate requires expensive model training.

papers.brief: VERAS wraps a general-purpose LLM coding agent with task-grounded verification: deterministic constraint observers, an isolated challenger agent to expose coverage gaps, and evidence-driven routing between feasibility repair, auditing, and objective improvement, with admission filtering to prevent regression. The key transferable idea is treating verification as evidence with declared coverage and using a fresh-context challenger to find shared specification blindness that self-checks miss — a practical mechanism for improving reliability in any LLM-driven program search.

This matters for OR/optimization methods applied to LLM inference infrastructure, but it is not a breakthrough for the team's primary evolutionary search agenda.

papers.title: T-GADE: Thermodynamical Generative-AI-Driven Evolution of LLM Artifacts
papers.affiliations: Osaka Metropolitan University

significance.reasoning: Directly relevant to LLM evolutionary search: the free-energy selection with temperature-controlled log-determinant diversity is a concrete, general alternative to standard truncation, and the HoxLM self-repair gives a sample-efficiency lever, with preregistered evidence on an EoH task. However, the sealed temperature benefit is only descriptive and the task is near saturation, so it is important to track but not field-changing.

papers.brief: Ogawa and Mori propose T-GADE, a free-energy selection framework for LLM-driven heuristic evolution that adds temperature-controlled log-determinant diversity, Fermi/Bose occupancy rules, and a per-individual self-repair step (HoxLM). On EoH's online bin-packing task with gpt-oss-20b, the HoxLM-equipped steady-state Fermi-type T=0 configuration beats EoH in 9/10 preregistered seed pairs at 400 total LLM calls (median sealed excess 0.836% vs 3.912%), though equal calls mask ~1.7x tokens per call. Temperature reliably controls population spread in both steady-state Fermi and generational Bose schemes, and a small positive temperature restores diversity in the generational case, but the sealed c100 gain is only descriptive after Holm adjustment. The key transferable idea is the log-determinant Gram-matrix free-energy objective with an explicit selection temperature, which provides a clean mechanism to trade off quality and diversity in LLM evolutionary search; the HoxLM self-repair step is reusable if a domain card is available. This matters for LLM evolutionary search because diversity control and local repair are two concrete instruments beyond standard EoH-style truncation.

papers.title: LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
papers.affiliations: IBM Research

significance.reasoning: The paper provides rigorous empirical evidence that proposal-based budgeting distorts LLM evolutionary search comparisons and that equal-token comparisons plus scorer audits erase most evolutionary advantages. This directly affects how we should design, report, and validate our evolutionary search results.

papers.brief: The paper replays 600 logged LLM evolutionary search runs across 5 tasks and 3 strategies, re-indexing performance by cumulative tokens instead of proposals. It shows proposal costs vary 16k-39k tokens, giving some methods up to 1.9x more compute in equal-proposal comparisons, and independent sampling is roughly 6x cheaper per attempt. When matched by token budget and after re-execution audits remove scorer exploits, evolution beats sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 pairs, with a 23-28% margin only on Heilbronn. The key takeaway is that token-level accounting and program audits should become standard reporting practice for LLM evolutionary search, because the proposal is not a unit of compute. This matters for anyone building or evaluating these systems, as much of the reported evolutionary advantage may be an accounting artifact.

papers.title: Evolving in Thought Space: Training a Small Model at Test Time Unlocks Better Discoveries
papers.affiliations: MIT, Hong Kong Polytechnic University, ByteDance, NUS, Stanford, University of Washington, UC Berkeley, Tsinghua, SMART

significance.reasoning: Directly advances test-time RL for LLM evolutionary search by decoupling strategy learning from execution, with strong benchmark gains and actionable ablations. Single-trajectory evidence limits causal strength, but the core separation idea and cost reduction are worth adopting.

papers.brief: Guidance-TTT trains a compact guidance model at test time to propose parent-conditioned strategic changes, while a frozen large execution model implements them, using PUCT parent selection and adaptive group-relative RL. On polyomino packing, Lasso, AHC058, and TriMul it reports 1-40% improvements over prior published methods and a ~58% cost reduction versus directly training a 120B executor. The key insight is separating 'what to change' from 'how to implement' so the RL signal concentrates on short high-level decisions and avoids expensive large-model adaptation. It also surfaces two important failure modes: outcome rewards conflate guidance quality with executor failures, and PUCT/policy updates can over-concentrate search in a few lineages. This directly informs sample-efficient and cost-effective designs in LLM-driven algorithm discovery.

papers.title: EPOCH: Coverage-Aware Evolution with Experiential Preference Optimization for LLM-based Automated Heuristic Design

significance.reasoning: Directly relevant strong empirical results in LLM evolutionary heuristic design; would likely inform but not fundamentally alter our approach, as it combines existing EoH-S/CALM/RPO components rather than introducing a field-changing method.

papers.brief: Gungordu et al. propose EPOCH, which fine-tunes an open LLM generator during evolutionary search using a per-instance optimality-gap representation to drive coverage-aware parent selection, operator allocation, and stagnation recovery; teacher reflection is converted into DPO preference pairs plus a reflective self-distillation term. This matters for LLM evolutionary algorithm design because it demonstrates a practical way to make fine-tuning and reflection accumulate across search iterations. The paper is under review and code is not released, but the methodology is concrete enough to implement.

papers.affiliations: Google, UC Berkeley, Stanford University

significance.reasoning: DuoDiscover directly targets sample efficiency and evaluator design in LLM evolutionary search, a core focus, with strong quantitative gains over AlphaEvolve-based baselines and a concrete transferable mechanism (co-discovered yardsticks with online fidelity testing). This warrants reconsidering how we treat evaluators in our own search frameworks.

papers.brief: DuoDiscover introduces a fleet of LLM coding agents that jointly discover an optimization target and a cheap proxy evaluator (yardstick), then hill-climb the yardstick while an orchestrator validates rank fidelity against true evaluations using Kendall-tau and coordinates agents. Key insight: under expensive evaluation, search should co-optimize what to evaluate and how to evaluate it cheaply, with continuous fidelity tests to prevent proxy drift; this is directly transferable to LLM evolutionary search. Results are backed by controlled budgets, baselines, and variance analysis, though no code is released. This matters because it addresses a central bottleneck in scaling LLM-driven discovery to real-world systems.

papers.title: Vesta: Queueing-Aware LLM Scheduling for Real-World Workloads
papers.affiliations: Tencent, The Chinese University of Hong Kong

significance.reasoning: Directly relevant to OR-based LLM serving scheduling; strong production-trace results justify discussing whether to incorporate queueing-externality pricing into existing scheduling formulations, but single-run evaluation and lack of code/variance temper its must-read status.

papers.brief: Zou et al. present Vesta, a queueing-aware scheduler for distributed agentic LLM serving that separates stable hashed KV-cache holders from per-request executors and prices the queueing externality of each placement via an M/M/c-derived congestion function. The key transferable idea is to charge only the incremental service demand beyond the cheapest candidate using a utilization- and Erlang-waiting-probability-based price, which automatically favors migration under slack and locality under congestion. This is directly useful for OR-based LLM serving scheduling and should be considered when formulating cluster-scheduling objectives, though the paper lacks released code and repeated-run variance.

papers.affiliations: Pennsylvania State University

significance.reasoning: The paper gives a solid empirical carbon–SLO characterization for geo-distributed LLM serving using a calibrated simulator and a batch-aware facility MILP, but the techniques are incremental adaptations of ILP/facility-location and existing serving simulation; it does not change how we approach LLM evolutionary search or multi-agent optimization.

papers.brief: Topcu et al. build a hardware-calibrated geo-distributed LLM serving simulator that models continuous batching, queueing, and per-phase power, and evaluate four carbon-aware schedulers including a facility MILP that prices batched energy collectively. The key useful idea is to use engine-level active batch load and queue depth to estimate TTFT/TPOT at scheduling time, and to charge per-datacenter fixed energy as a facility cost in a MILP, which gives a strong carbon–SLO balance. This is relevant for LLM serving scheduling and batch resource allocation, though it is not a fundamental advance for LLM evolutionary search or multi-agent optimization.

papers.brief: FDE-Bench evaluates 49 real customer cases (29 combinatorial optimization, 20 machine learning) where agents must ask a simulated customer to clarify underspecified business requirements, then iteratively optimize a deliverable scored against customer-accepted reference solutions. significance.reasoning: OPT-Kraken is a well-executed post-hoc repair framework with strong empirical coverage across six benchmarks and eight upstream generators, but it targets LLM OR modeling repair rather than our core LLM evolutionary search or process reward model work. The artifact-fidelity versus outcome-accuracy gap and contract-constrained local repair are directly relevant to LLM-based OR modeling evaluation and merit a discussion on incorporating repair/fidelity checks there.

papers.brief: OPT-Kraken is a training-free post-hoc framework that detects and repairs hallucinations in LLM-generated optimization models and solver code by extracting requirements and instance data, running directional fidelity checks, selecting minimal repair scope, and applying contract-constrained local edits with artifact-level audit and safe commit. Results across six OR benchmarks and eight upstream generators show 4.1–20.1 percentage point accuracy gains with regression at or below 1.1%, and controlled ablations support each mechanism. The key transferable idea is treating repair as evidence-grounded and scope-controlled, with protected content and deterministic commit gates rather than open-ended regeneration. This matters for LLM-based OR modeling and evaluation because outcome accuracy can mask unfaithful artifacts, and post-hoc repair can improve fidelity without retraining. For our work, it is complementary: most useful for LLM OR modeling evaluation and verification rather than core evolutionary search or multi-agent optimization.

papers.brief: GAL alternates a GEPA-based discriminator that generates adversarial evaluation examples with a Cursor/Claude generator that evolves approximation algorithms for KV compression, sparse decoding, sparse video generation, and context extension. papers.affiliations: Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen University

significance.reasoning: MECo directly addresses cross-problem generalization in LLM-driven heuristic design with strong results on VRP/FJSP and introduces reusable transfer-gap and complementary-set mechanisms. It warrants team review for possible integration into LLM evolutionary search pipelines, though it does not alter core fitness/sample-efficiency thinking.

papers.brief: Xie et al. propose MECo, an LLM multi-task evolutionary framework that evolves task-conditioned heuristic populations on single-constraint source tasks and recombines them into combined tasks, using a population-level transfer gap to choose parent pairs and a complementary set-selection criterion to select four heuristics for zero-shot use. Across 16 VRP and 16 FJSP variants, it achieves lower out-of-domain costs than eight AHD baselines (e.g., VRP OOD 22.11 vs MoH 22.55; FJSP OOD 1474.4 vs MoH 1487.3), and integrating it with EoH, ReEvo, and HSEvo improves their ID/OOD performance. The key insight is that source-only feedback can support robust cross-problem generalization by measuring empirical transfer gaps between task populations and selecting a complementary portfolio across source-task combinations. This is directly relevant to LLM evolutionary heuristic design, though its current scope is specialized to constraint-compositional VRP/FJSP families.

papers.title: AGAR: a reinforcement learning substrate for LLM program evolution
papers.affiliations: Baidu, Tsinghua University, University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Institute of Automation Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai University

significance.reasoning: Directly relevant to LLM evolutionary search and conceptually novel, but empirical evidence is provisional: n=3, no per-module ablation, 2-4x LLM budget, and no code release. The formalization is worth discussing for RL-infused evolution, but it does not yet compel a change in approach.

papers.brief: AGAR formalizes LLM program evolution as an MDP whose action is the modular text prefix, letting RL tools (credit assignment, value estimation, adaptive exploration, memory) attach as swappable modules without gradient training; it also introduces a modular TextGrad local-edit operator and characterizes asynchronous staleness. On 19 tasks with two backends and three seeds, AGAR improves normalized scores over OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve (e.g. 0.949/0.990 vs 0.855/0.919 on DeepSeek) and shows +14.6% end-to-end over a bare loop, though gains concentrate on competitive-programming tasks and statistical rigor is limited. The key insight is that treating the conditioning prefix, not the emitted program, as the action makes Bellman recursion well-posed and turns each hand-set evolutionary constant into a replaceable estimator, yielding a clean γ=0 reading of prior systems. This matters for LLM evolutionary search because it offers an auditable factorization for RL-infused evolution, but the empirical gains and code remain to be verified.

papers.title: Discovered, Not Designed: Population Evolution for Collaborative and Compute-Intensive Model Discovery
papers.affiliations: Meta

significance.reasoning: Strong empirical evidence that shared ledgers and cross-instance replay improve LLM evolutionary search across recommendation, RL, and pretraining; directly relevant to collaborative evolutionary search, but lacks code and has single-run limitations, so it does not force a change in approach.

papers.brief: Peng et al. propose Population Evolution (PE), a collaborative, hierarchical framework for LLM-driven model discovery that shares executable interventions and cross-instance replay results across related search instances, and screens candidates on small training subsets before full-target evaluation. Results are backed by concrete numbers: PE improves mean best local gains from 7.01% to 8.97% on ranking and 2.84% to 3.85% on watch-time, raises best larger-scale outcomes in all five task families, and under matched GPU compute yields 2.48% vs 0.92% best LLM gain and 13 vs 0 successful candidates. The key transferable idea is using a shared ledger of weak and successful peer evaluations as proposal context to reuse, modify, or combine mechanisms across instances while keeping local archives separate. This matters for LLM evolutionary search because it shows cross-instance sharing and hierarchical screening can improve both sample efficiency and full-target outcomes on expensive tasks.

papers.title: Harnessing LLMs with Direction-Scope Control for Combinatorial Solver Refinement
papers.affiliations: Nankai University, University of Waterloo, JD.com

significance.reasoning: Directly addresses stability and token efficiency in LLM-driven heuristic refinement, a core issue for LLM evolutionary search. The direction-scope harness and failure-group distillation are concrete techniques with strong multi-benchmark results that the team should evaluate for integration.

papers.brief: Cao et al. introduce DiSH, a harness for LLM-based solver refinement that jointly controls revision scope via feasibility pass rate and revision direction via failure-group distillation, evaluated on nine combinatorial optimization benchmarks across four LLMs. Results show consistent QYI gains (average 80.3 vs. 67.4 for HeuriGym) and roughly halved feedback tokens, supported by controlled ablations and multiple baselines. Key insight: explicitly narrowing revision scope as feasibility accumulates prevents regressions, while grouping normalized error signatures cuts redundant feedback without sacrificing repair effectiveness. This matters for LLM evolutionary search because stable iterative code refinement is a central challenge, and the scope-direction control could be transferred to population-based evolutionary harnesses.

methodology.novelty_claim: First AHD harness to jointly control revision direction (representative failure-group evidence) and revision scope (feasibility-conditioned semantic revision levels) before LLM generation to suppress feasibility oscillation.

papers.title: JOVE: Joint Execution and Verification for Resource-Aware LLM Task Graphs
papers.affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, DEVCOM Army Research Laboratory

significance.reasoning: The MILP-plus-LinUCB formulation and D-optimal selective-verification bonus are directly relevant to LLM serving resource allocation and process reward model label acquisition; the team should evaluate whether this online verification-aware allocation can be adapted, though it does not change our core LLM evolutionary search approach.

papers.brief: Zhang et al. propose an online MILP framework that jointly assigns executor LLMs to task-graph nodes and chooses which node outputs to pay to verify, under a long-term average API-cost budget and per-query latency chance constraints. On four reasoning benchmarks, JOVE reports accuracy comparable to unconstrained baselines while using 3.7–16.3x lower cost and 8.3–17.0x lower latency, though results are mean ± std over only three random orderings with no significance tests. The key transferable idea is the D-optimal information-gain bonus that makes verification a decision variable: a node is verified when the expected reduction in parameter uncertainty exceeds its priced verification cost, enabling selective paid feedback to improve future allocations. This matters for resource-constrained LLM serving, task-graph orchestration, and active selection of process reward labels in multi-agent optimization.

papers.brief: FrugalEvo proposes cost-aware LLM evolutionary search: a high-cost LLM generates design strategies, a low-cost LLM implements/refines code, with cache-efficient prompts, evaluated via a new Budget-Aware AUC metric. The key takeaway is decoupling strategy exploration from implementation using strong/weak model pairs and measuring best-so-far score against cumulative cost, which is a practical way to improve sample/cost efficiency in LLM evolutionary search. This matters for the LLM evolutionary search area because cost-aware evaluation and multi-model orchestration are directly actionable for resource-constrained discovery workflows.

papers.brief: SEDIMA adds a persistent three-level memory to LLM evolutionary search: raw traces, LLM-distilled insights, and attention-weighted semantic clusters, retrieved by embedding similarity and injected into mutation prompts without changing search operators. The key takeaway is that cross-run semantic retrieval of distilled optimization insights—rather than lineage-based or prompt-only memory—yields consistent gains and transfers across problem families. This is relevant for any LLM evolutionary search system needing persistent memory and sample efficiency.

papers.title: Autoresearch in Mixed-Integer Linear and Nonlinear Programming
papers.affiliations: Singapore Management University, Eindhoven University of Technology, Nanyang Technological University, Shandong University, Chengdu University of Information Technology

significance.reasoning: AutoMIP introduces a concrete persistent idea-pool + algorithm-tree mechanism with artifact-compatible parent selection that directly addresses long-horizon memory and sample efficiency in LLM evolutionary search; its strong MIPLib/MINLPLib wins over EoH-style baselines make it a relevant reference for our algorithm-design and MIP projects.

papers.brief: AutoMIP is an LLM autoresearch framework for MILP/MINLP that couples a persistent idea pool with a multiway algorithm tree; at each step it jointly selects a research direction and a compatible historical state whose saved artifacts are restored, enabling backtracking and reuse of accumulated work. On MIPLib Open/Hard and MINLPLib it reports higher success rates and faster completion than Codex, Loop, AutoEoH, and EvoX, along with materially lower token usage; these results are backed by per-instance outcomes and an ablation showing both idea pooling and tree state reuse contribute. The key transferable idea is to treat experimental state as reusable artifacts linked to candidate ideas, with explicit L-refinement/R-switch edges and compatibility checks, rather than evolving a population of independent programs. This matters for long-horizon LLM evolutionary search because it directly addresses stagnation and sample efficiency, though the paper currently lacks released code and uses limited statistical repetition.

methodology.core_method: LLM autoresearch agent skill coupling a persistent idea pool (PoolThink) with a multiway algorithm tree (L refinement / R direction-switch edges) and artifact-compatible parent-state restoration, plus a verification layer
methodology.novelty_claim: Jointly selects the next research direction and its compatible historical starting state by coupling a persistent idea pool with an algorithm tree that stores reusable executable artifacts.

papers.title: Right Answers, Costly Models: The Efficiency Gap in LLM-based Optimization Modeling
papers.affiliations: Peking University, Beijing Jiaotong University, Beihang University, Great Bay University

significance.reasoning: This paper is directly relevant to LLM optimization modeling evaluation, with solid empirical evidence that correctness and model compactness are insufficient without solver-cost and construction-cost comparisons. It could inform how we evaluate LLM-generated optimization models, but it does not change our primary LLM evolutionary search methods.

papers.brief: This paper introduces OptTips, a catalog of 50 expert optimization modeling techniques, and OptDachshund, a multi-agent pipeline that builds EfficientOpt: 561 tasks with paired conventional and expert reference formulations on identical data. It evaluates 11 LLMs and shows that correct objective values often come with 1.5–2× higher solver runtime than expert references, that smaller formulations can still solve slower, and that model construction overhead can offset faster solving. Results are backed by Gurobi measurements on over 4,000 correct runs and multiple cost metrics, not just claims. The key takeaway is that LLM optimization modeling benchmarks should evaluate computational efficiency and technique use via paired expert references, not correctness alone. This matters for LLM-driven optimization modeling evaluation, especially where generated models are used in real solver workflows, and suggests incorporating solver/construction cost comparisons into our own evaluation practices.

methodology.core_method: Multi-agent LLM pipeline (OptDachshund: technique matcher, reformulation designer, quality auditor, repair agent, reference implementation agent, reference audit agent) guided by a 50-card expert technique knowledge base (OptTips) to build paired ordinary/expert reference models; evaluation of 11 LLMs generating Gurobi solver code

methodology.novelty_claim: First expert-curated technique catalog (OptTips) used to construct a benchmark (EfficientOpt) with paired ordinary/expert references on identical data, enabling separate evaluation of correctness, technique use, and computational cost of LLM-generated optimization models.

papers.title: Toward Quantum Software Automation: A Quantum-Aware Harness for LLM-Guided Evolution
papers.affiliations: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign

significance.reasoning: The paper is domain-specific to quantum software, so it does not change our core approach. However, the evolution-hardness-guided coreset and task-specific policy reward are concrete, transferable techniques for reducing evaluation cost and improving reward shaping in LLM evolutionary search, warranting a team discussion on adapting them to our benchmark evaluation pipelines.

papers.brief: Wan et al. present QSA, a quantum-aware harness that wraps an OpenEvolve-style LLM evolutionary loop with domain-specific verification, prompting, and reward mechanisms, evaluated on IBM QPUs for quantum error mitigation and multiprogramming. Results are hardware-backed: QSA improves QPU utilization by 4.2–9.5% and fidelity by 15.2–19.5% over QOS, while reducing mitigation time by at least 96.8% with comparable fidelity, at a reported LLM API cost of $6.9 over 11.3 hours. The most transferable insight is evolution-hardness-guided coreset extraction: run preliminary evolution on uniformly sampled verification sets, identify the scale where evolved programs perform worst, and focus the compact verification set there, improving full-suite reward from −0.08 to 0.12 compared with random coresets. Also notable is the policy reward combining Pareto rank from non-dominated sorting with Pearson correlation to ground-truth rankings, providing denser guidance for multi-objective runtime policies. While the quantum software problem is outside our core domains, these techniques directly address evaluation cost and reward feedback in LLM evolutionary search and are worth considering for transfer.

methodology.core_method: OpenEvolve LLM-guided evolutionary program search wrapped in a quantum-aware harness: evolution-hardness-guided coreset extraction, proxy (depth/CNOT/relative-balance) scoring, static+snapshot analysis prompting, and task-specific rewards (weighted circuit reward; Pareto-rank + Pearson-correlation policy reward)
methodology.llm_model_used: Gemini 3 Pro (default); also Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5.3-Codex, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.6
methodology.novelty_claim: A quantum-aware harness that supplies domain-specific verification (hardness-guided coreset + proxy scoring), prompting (static/snapshot analysis), and reward design (Pareto-rank + correlation policy reward) to generic LLM-guided evolutionary search for quantum compiler passes and runtime policies.

papers.title: Self-Evolving Algorithm-Design Agents: Escaping In-Context Evolutionary Stagnation via Population-Curated Policy Optimization
papers.affiliations: Nanjing University, Huawei Noah's Ark Lab

significance.reasoning: Directly targets sample-efficient parametric evolution for LLM algorithm design with strong quantitative gains over in-context evolutionary baselines; the hybrid on/off-policy population curation is actionable even if no significance tests or code are provided.

papers.brief: Lu et al. propose Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO), which maintains a curated global population of self-generated algorithms and alternates refreshing on-policy GRPO with regularized off-policy updates on top-k elites. On 16 global placement chip cases trained on only 4, PCPO outperforms OpenEvolve and ShinkaEvolve, beats GRPO, and matches GPT-5.5; on 4 GPU kernels it averages 8.27x speedup over PyTorch Eager. Results are backed by benchmark tables and strong baselines, though no significance tests or released code are provided. The key insight is that pure in-context evolutionary search can stagnate by reinforcing misleading self-generated context, and parametric population-curated RL with hybrid updates can internalize domain knowledge and improve sample efficiency. This is relevant for LLM evolutionary search, especially sample-efficiency and RL-infused evolution directions.

methodology.core_method: Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO): GRPO-based hybrid policy update combining refreshing on-policy GRPO with periodic regularized off-policy GRPO over a curated global population (AST dedup, semantic twin removal, illegal filtering, intra-bucket reward normalization, policy-level diversity, top-k nonnegative ranking advantage, clipped importance ratios + KL to reference policy)
methodology.novelty_claim: Sample-efficient parametric self-evolution of algorithm-design agents via a curated global population with hybrid on/off-policy RL updates, motivated by an Improvement Chain local-likelihood-transfer proposition.
components: clipped off-policy GRPO with KL regularization
